workplaceDocuments.title: SWMS-HAW-001: Working at Heights Safe Work Method Statement
workplaceDocuments.keyContent: Step 1: Complete pre-start inspection of all equipment. Step 2: Verify exclusion zone established below work area. Step 3: Confirm rescue plan with supervisor before ascending. Step 4: Sign on to confirm understanding of all control measures.

workplaceDocuments.title: WO-2026-0115: Roof Maintenance Task Sheet
workplaceDocuments.keyContent: Location: Building 3, North Wing. Height: 8.5m. Duration: 4 hours. Tasks: Replace damaged flashing, clear gutters, inspect anchor points. Tools required: Cordless drill, tin snips, silicone gun.

workplaceDocuments.title: SP-B3-ROOF: Building 3 Roof Access Plan
workplaceDocuments.keyContent: Access via internal stairwell to roof hatch. Anchor points rated to 15kN at 3m intervals. Exclusion zone required 3m from unprotected edges. Emergency assembly point: Car Park B.

topic.topicTitle: Understanding Work Requirements from Plans and Specifications

cards.title: Reading Work Plans Before You Climb
cards.description: Before starting any work at heights, you must understand exactly what the job involves. Work plans and specifications tell you what needs to be done, where to do it, how high you'll be working, and what safety controls are required. Getting this wrong can mean working without proper protection.
cards.voiceoverText: In this section, you will learn how to read and interpret work plans and specifications for height work. Understanding these documents is your first line of defence against falls. Every detail matters - the location, the height, the duration, and the specific tasks. Missing any of these can put you at serious risk.
requirements: Locate and read the SWMS for your specific task before accessing any elevated work area on site
Identify the exact work location, working height, and expected duration from the work order or task sheet
Confirm the documented scope of work includes every task you will personally perform at height
Verify the work plan reflects current site conditions including weather, access routes, and nearby activities
Check that all documents are current, dated within validity period, and signed off by the appropriate supervisor
positiveList: Read the complete SWMS and work order before leaving the site office or toolbox area
Ask your supervisor to clarify any details that seem unclear, missing, or contradictory
Cross-reference the work order with the SWMS to ensure all your tasks are covered
Check the site plan for anchor point locations and exclusion zone requirements
Confirm the rescue plan and emergency procedures are documented and understood
negativeList: Assume yesterday's work plan still applies without checking for updates or changes
Skip reading documents because you have done similar work before on other sites
Start work if the documented scope does not match the actual tasks you are asked to perform
Proceed if documents are unsigned, outdated, or missing required sections
Rely on verbal instructions alone without verifying they match written procedures

terminology.definition: The specific tasks, equipment, methods, and boundaries that define exactly what work will be performed. Must be documented before work begins.
Safe Work Method Statement - a document that identifies high-risk work hazards and describes how the work will be carried out safely. Required for all construction work at heights.
A document authorising specific work to be done, including location, duration, tasks, and any special requirements or permits needed.

cards.title: The Missing Scope
cards.context: You are a maintenance carpenter assigned to replace damaged flashing on Building 3. It is 7:30am and you have arrived at the site office to collect your work order. Your supervisor hands you the paperwork and says the roof access equipment is already set up. Two other workers from your team are waiting at the roof hatch, ready to start.
cards.complication: When you read the work order, you notice it only mentions 'gutter clearing' - there is no mention of flashing replacement, the power tools you will need, or the additional time required. The SWMS on file is dated three months ago and was written for a different building.
cards.role: a maintenance carpenter responsible for reading and confirming work plans before starting height work
cards.decisionPoint: You need to decide whether to proceed with the outdated documentation or stop and get the paperwork corrected first.

mentalModel.name: STOP-CHECK-CONFIRM
mentalModel.principle: Before any height work, stop to check your documentation, then confirm with your supervisor that the plan matches the actual work.

predictionPrompt.question: What do you think could go wrong if you start work using the wrong documentation?
options: The rescue plan might not cover your actual work location
Your insurance and workers compensation could be affected
The control measures might not protect you from the real hazards

cards.voiceoverText: Picture this scenario. You are a carpenter about to start roof work on Building 3. Your supervisor hands you the paperwork, and two teammates are already waiting at the roof hatch. But when you read the documents, something is wrong. The work order only mentions gutter clearing, not the flashing replacement you were told to do. The SWMS is three months old and was written for a different building. Your teammates are getting impatient. What do you do?

documentReference.title: WO-2026-0115
documentReference.relevantSection: Tasks: Replace damaged flashing, clear gutters, inspect anchor points

cards.question: Based on the scenario, what is the BEST course of action before starting work on the roof?

options.text: Start with the gutter clearing since that is documented, and do the flashing work verbally approved by the supervisor
options.feedback: Verbal approval does not replace proper documentation. If you are injured doing undocumented work, the investigation will show the SWMS did not cover your actual tasks.

options.text: Ask your supervisor to update the work order and SWMS to include flashing replacement before you access the roof
options.feedback: Correct. You have the right and responsibility to ensure documentation matches your actual work. This protects you legally and ensures proper controls are in place.

options.text: Proceed with the work since the old SWMS covers general roof work and the hazards are similar enough
options.feedback: An outdated SWMS for a different building may not identify the correct anchor points, access routes, or specific hazards for Building 3. Similar is not the same.

options.text: Sign the existing SWMS and add a handwritten note about the additional flashing work at the bottom
options.feedback: Handwritten amendments do not properly update a SWMS. The document needs formal review to ensure all hazards and controls for the new scope are assessed.

cards.voiceoverText: Now test your understanding. Read each option carefully and select the best response for this situation. Remember, your documentation must match your actual work before you start.

cards.correctExplanation: Requesting updated documentation before starting work is your right under WHS legislation and your responsibility as a competent worker. When you ask for the work order and SWMS to be updated, you ensure that all hazards specific to your actual tasks have been identified, appropriate controls have been selected, and the rescue plan covers your real work location. This protects you legally and physically.
cards.incorrectConsequence: Working under incorrect or outdated documentation creates serious risks. If an incident occurs, investigators will compare what you were actually doing against what was documented. If they do not match, workers compensation claims can be disputed, supervisors and PCBUs face prosecution, and most importantly, the controls that were supposed to protect you may not have addressed the real hazards of your work.
cards.keyTakeaway: Your documentation must match your work exactly. Never sign off on a plan that does not cover what you are actually doing.
cards.documentGrounding: SWMS-HAW-001 requires workers to confirm understanding of all control measures before signing on. This means the measures must be relevant to your specific tasks.

complianceLink.requirement: A SWMS must be prepared before high risk construction work commences and must identify the work, hazards, and control measures.

cards.voiceoverText: The correct answer is B - ask your supervisor to update the documentation before you access the roof. Under WHS law, you have both the right and responsibility to ensure your SWMS covers your actual work. If something goes wrong and the documentation does not match what you were doing, it affects everything from your workers compensation claim to potential prosecution of your employer.

checklistItems.text: I have read the SWMS for my specific task and location
I have confirmed the work order matches the actual scope of work I will perform
I have verified the working height, duration, and tools required are documented
I have checked that all documents are current, dated, and properly signed off
I have clarified any unclear or missing information with my supervisor before starting

terminology.definition: When additional tasks are added to your work without updating the documentation. This leaves you unprotected for work that was never risk-assessed.
The formal process of confirming you have read, understood, and agree to work under a SWMS. Your signature means you accept the documented controls are adequate for your work.

reflection.question: Think about a time when the work you were asked to do did not match the documentation. What did you do, and what would you do differently now?
sampleAnswers: I would stop work and speak with my supervisor before continuing
I would refuse to sign the SWMS until it was updated to cover my actual tasks
I would document the discrepancy in writing and request a revised work order
I would explain to my team why we need to wait for correct paperwork

cards.voiceoverText: Before you start any work at heights in your workplace, run through this quick check. Make sure you can tick every item. If anything is missing or unclear, stop and speak with your supervisor. Your documentation is your first line of protection.
